# Mirrik

> Play the same sound on two or more output devices at once, on Windows and Linux,
> without ever creating a virtual audio device.

Mirrik captures whatever your computer is already playing and sends a copy to as many
outputs as you pick: speakers and headphones together, two headsets for one film, game
audio shared with the person next to you, or sound piped into a second room over HDMI.
There is nothing to configure first — no virtual audio cable, no extra driver. Run it when
you need it, close it, and the system is exactly as clean as before.

The distinguishing property: **no virtual device is ever created.** Unlike virtual audio
cables, Voicemeeter or `combine-sink`, there is no fake device to select, remember or
clean up, your default output is never changed, and other programs notice nothing. Turn
it off and nothing is left behind.

- Version: 0.1.1
- Licence: MIT
- Language: Rust (GUI in egui/eframe)
- Repository: https://github.com/Kris-023/mirrik
- Landing page: https://kris-023.github.io/mirrik/

## Platform support

| Platform | Supported | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Windows 10 / 11 | yes | WASAPI loopback capture, render client per destination |
| Linux (PipeWire) | yes | `module-loopback` tapping the monitor of the current sink |
| Linux (PulseAudio only) | no | Refused deliberately: a crash would strand a loopback permanently |
| macOS | not yet | No backend written |

PipeWire's PulseAudio compatibility layer is fine; only plain PulseAudio is refused.

## Capabilities

- Mirror to an unlimited number of destinations, added and removed one at a time, while
  everything else keeps playing.
- Analogue, USB, HDMI and Bluetooth outputs can be mixed freely. Mismatched sample rates
  are converted on the fly (a 192 kHz output can feed a 48 kHz headset).
- Independent volume per destination. Faders apply after the point where the copy is
  taken, so levels are genuinely separate. If a driver applies gain before that point,
  the window says so rather than pretending to be in control.
- Survives change: switching the main output mid-session makes the mirror follow, and an
  unplugged destination is kept listed. It rejoins by itself while the window is open;
  with no window open and no command running, the next one picks it back up. Nothing of
  Mirrik watches for devices on its own.
- Automatic light / OLED theming, taken from the system's light-dark setting. On Windows
  the choice is fixed at window open, because Windows only reports it once at launch.
- Clock drift between devices is corrected continuously; over many hours the only trace
  is an occasional faint tick.
- The set that was last on is remembered across a reboot, but never restored on its own:
  the window offers it and `Space` takes it. Mirroring stays a deliberate action.

## Latency

- Mirrored destination runs ~30 ms behind the original on Windows, ~42 ms on Linux.
  Measured per destination, not estimated, and displayed in the window.
- Bluetooth destinations add roughly 200 ms of their own buffering on top, and are
  labelled as such in the interface.

## Installing

Linux, guided:

    git clone https://github.com/Kris-023/mirrik.git
    cd mirrik
    ./install.sh

Requires PipeWire (check with `pactl info | grep 'Server Name'`) and the tools `pactl`,
`pw-cli`, `pw-dump`, `pw-metadata`. No root. The script detects the compositor (Hyprland,
Sway, i3, GNOME, KDE and others) to set up a hotkey, and recognises Debian, Ubuntu,
Fedora including rpm-ostree, Arch, openSUSE, Alpine, Void, Gentoo and NixOS for package
hints. It has no `--uninstall` flag on purpose: it only ever prints commands for you to
run yourself.

Windows, guided:

    powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File install.ps1

No admin rights. Verify the download against the published `SHA256SUMS` first with
`Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256`. The binaries are not code-signed, so SmartScreen will
warn; choose "More info", then "Run anyway". Uninstall with `-Uninstall`, which shows
everything it found before removing any of it.

From source:

    cargo build --release

Rust 1.95 or newer, a floor set by egui/eframe rather than Mirrik. The workspace holds
five crates: `core`, `backend-linux`, `backend-windows`, `cli`, `gui`. The two backend
crates are separate, so a plain `cargo build` only pulls in the one matching the host OS.

## Keyboard

The window is fully keyboard-driven.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `Down` `Up` or `j` `k` | Move focus; faders and devices share one chain |
| `Right` `Left` or `l` `h` | Nudge the focused fader in 5% steps |
| `1` … `9` | Switch that device on or off directly |
| `Enter` | On a device: add it, or remove it if already active |
| `Space` | Mirror to the set used last time; only offered while nothing is running |
| `x` | Stop mirroring everywhere |
| `Esc` or `q` | Close the window; the mirror keeps running |

Closing the window does not stop the mirror. Only `x` does.

`Space` re-applies the last set of destinations. It is offered, never applied on its own:
the rows say "from last time" and stay off until the key is pressed. A device from that
set that is currently unplugged is waited for and joins as soon as it appears, for as long
as the window stays open — nothing of Mirrik watches for devices on its own, so the wait
ends with it. (The per-destination holder processes below are a different thing: they exist
only while the mirror is running, and they watch nothing.)

## Command line

    mirrik devices                  # list outputs, * marks the current one
    mirrik on airpods               # start mirroring to one device
    mirrik on airpods hdmi          # ... or several at once
    mirrik add speakers             # add one more while running
    mirrik remove hdmi              # drop one, keep the rest
    mirrik toggle airpods           # add if absent, remove if present
    mirrik status                   # what is running
    mirrik off                      # stop everything
    mirrik volume airpods 60        # read or set a device's volume, 0-100

Device names match on any unique substring, and an ambiguous match is reported rather
than guessed. Every subcommand that reports something accepts `--json`.
`mirrik status --quiet` exits 0 while mirroring and 1 otherwise, for shell conditions.

## Design guarantees

Each mirrored destination is held open by its own small background process. That is what
makes "off means gone" a guarantee rather than a promise: if the process dies for any
reason, the destination disappears with it. Nothing can outlive a crash.
